surveyDefinition.title: Running Shoes — consumer survey (Canada)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, train for events, prioritise cushioning, durability and fit over price. Willing to pay premium for technology and performance.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Run occasionally or for fitness, but are highly constrained by price. They wait for sales, buy last season's models, and often abandon purchase if over $100.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Consumers
segments.description: Value sustainability and ethical production highly. Willing to pay a premium for eco-friendly materials, but only if performance and comfort are not compromised.

segments.name: Casual Lifestyle Users
segments.description: Run occasionally or use running shoes for casual wear and commuting. Low engagement with performance features, more driven by style, comfort and brand reputation.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Running Shoes buyers in Canada. It asks how people use Running Shoes, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in Canada who buy or use Running Shoes for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. Excluded: Professional athletes whose shoes are provided by sponsors; Businesses purchasing shoes for employees or resale; Children under 18 (unless purchasing for themselves, but typically parent decides).
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Engages in running or jogging at least occasionally
Purchases athletic footwear for fitness, sport, or casual wear
Researches brands, reviews, and features before buying
May be brand loyal or open to switching based on price/performance
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are modelled estimates built from published market evidence — they are not measurements from fielded interviews, and should be read as an expected shape of response rather than a result. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — from frequency and context to shoe ownership and fit confidence. It then traces the purchase journey: what triggers a new pair, how they research, where they buy, how often they replace, and what they pay. Next, it probes their preferences and expectations: must-have features, quality signals, sustainability priorities, trade-offs, and value perception. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future intentions. This arc separates the four segments by their running intensity, price…

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Running Shoes in Canada — who Individuals who have bought running shoes in the past 12 months; Individuals who run or exercise regularly (at least once a week); Individuals who are the primary decision-maker for their own shoe purchase. The survey targets the end consumer who buys and uses running shoes for personal fitness and lifestyle. This audience represents the primary market for running shoes globally.

metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on running frequency, purchase drivers, price sensitivity, and sustainability orientation.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Combination of usage/behavioural and price sensitivity: the category separates primarily on how often and how seriously people run (which drives their needs) and how much price constrains their choices (given high price sensitivity in the mid-range). This combination best captures the real differenc

segments.name: Performance-Focused Runners
segments.description: Run multiple times per week, train for events, prioritise cushioning, durability and fit over price. Willing to pay premium for technology and performance.
segments.hypothesis: They replace shoes every 300-500 miles, buy from specialty running stores, and are driven by comfort and performance features rather than price.

segments.name: Price-Sensitive Buyers
segments.description: Run occasionally or for fitness, but are highly constrained by price. They wait for sales, buy last season's models, and often abandon purchase if over $100.
segments.hypothesis: They are most likely to cite price as a top driver, buy on discount or from mass merchants, and have a longer replacement cycle.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Consumers
segments.description: Value sustainability and ethical production highly. Willing to pay a premium for eco-friendly materials, but only if performance and comfort are not compromised.
segments.hypothesis: They actively seek out sustainable materials and certifications, and are more likely to switch brands for a greener option.

segments.name: Casual Lifestyle Users
segments.description: Run occasionally or use running shoes for casual wear and commuting. Low engagement with performance features, more driven by style, comfort and brand reputation.
segments.hypothesis: They buy less frequently, are influenced by fashion trends, and may not prioritise technical features or sustainability.

segmentModel.tie_break: The question 'Which of these best describes how you use your running shoes?' (cp2) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it explicitly categorizes usage into training, fitness, occasional, or casual, which aligns with the core definition of each segment.
notes: Eco-conscious segment is primarily identified through willingness to pay for eco materials (pe4) and ranking sustainable materials as important (bb8).
Price-sensitive segment is identified through price thresholds (bb6, bb7) and deal-seeking behavior (bb1, bb2).
Performance-focused segment is identified through high frequency and training behavior (cp2, cp5, cp6) and performance priorities (pe7).
Casual lifestyle segment is identified through low frequency and casual use (cp2, cp5) and style/comfort priorities (bb1, bb8).
6 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are modelled from published market evidence, not measured from fielded interviews. Replace them with primary data once the study is run.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey opens by establishing the respondent's relationship with running — from frequency and context to shoe ownership and fit confidence. It then traces the purchase journey: what triggers a new pair, how they research, where they buy, how often they replace, and what they pay. Next, it probes their preferences and expectations: must-have features, quality signals, sustainability priorities, trade-offs, and value perception. Finally, it measures satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future intentions. This arc separates the four segments by their running intensity, price…
storyline_notes: Added a beat on fit and sizing confidence in the consumer profile section, as fit is a critical issue in footwear and a key differentiator.
Replaced generic 'need state' with 'shoe ownership and rotation' to capture how many pairs they own and how they use them, which helps distinguish casual from serious runners.
In buying behavior, added a dedicated beat on replacement cycle, which is essential for running shoes and helps segment by usage intensity.
In preferences, added a beat on sustainability credentials to reflect the high environmental awareness in North America and the growing demand for eco-friendly materials.
In satisfaction, added a beat on pain points to capture the specific frustrations like high prices and difficulty balancing comfort and durability.
The canonical arc was adapted to focus on running-specific behaviours rather than generic category usage.
metadata.classification_reason: Everyday consumers buy running shoes for personal use, pay for them out of pocket, and decide which pair to purchase based on fit, style, and performance. While some businesses may purchase shoes for employees (e.g., athletic teams), the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
